To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) exposure to postdisaster violent, injurious and death-related traumatic events, (b) conflict with the caregiver, (c) caregiver unavailability to talk about the disaster, and (d) nonparticipation in a school-based mental health intervention were each associated with increased post-disaster child distress.

(1) children who experienced multiple disaster-related traumatic experiences were at increased risk for posttraumatic stress symptoms; (2) children’s perceptions of their caregiver’s unavailability to discuss their earthquake-related experiences were associated with increased post-disaster distress; and (3) participation in a school-based mental health program appeared to be protective for at risk children.
children’s exposure to traumatic experiences, family context, school environment, and school-based intervention were correlated with children’s earthquake-related psychological reactions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of family context and school-based mental healthcare in understanding children’s posttraumatic stress symptoms in response to the 2012 Chilean earthquake.
the effects of the 2012 earthquake in Sichuan, China on children’s posttraumatic stress symptoms.
the impact of the 2012 earthquake on children in the region of Pichilemu, Chile.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

this study provides support for the notion that children who are exposed to multiple traumatic events are at greater risk of developing posttraumatic stress symptoms and that children who perceive their caregivers as being unavailable to discuss their earthquake experiences are more likely to experience elevated postdisaster distress and worry.

this study found evidence of the protective effect of mental health interventions on the mental health of children exposed to the Chilean earthquake, as well as evidence that the family environment can be an important risk factor in children’s mental health post-disaster.
this study is an example of the value of a longitudinal, mixed method approach to the study of disaster impact on children and their families.

children’s exposure to multiple postdisaster traunas and negative family environment are associated with postdisaster distress, but school-based mental health intervention may be protective for these children.

children are at risk following a natural disaster.
